raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old male presented to the emergency room complaining of progressive dyspnea and productive cough over the course of 4 months. He also noted decreased appetite with a 50-pound weight loss over the past 5 months. He had no significant past medical or surgical history and was not taking any medications. His family history was unremarkable. He quit smoking tobacco two months ago due to worsening respiratory status; he rarely used alcohol and never used recreational drugs. He was unmarried and in a long-term heterosexual relationship and denied multiple sexual partners. He was currently working in an automobile parts factory as a janitor. After high school he had enlisted in the army and served for four years; at that time he was stationed in Hawaii. While in Hawaii he visited a single prostitute on several occasions.
Initial vital signs revealed temperature was 99.9 F, blood pressure 128/83 mmHg, pulse 134 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 22 breaths/minute; oxygen saturation was 92% on room air. He was in moderate respiratory distress, yet was awake, alert, and cooperative. Extraocular muscles were intact; there was no nystagmus or scleral icterus. Pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light. He had thrush under his tongue and on the palate. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy. Heart rate was regular with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops by auscultation. There were no palpable thrills. He had equal chest rise bilaterally. Breath sounds were diminished throughout, with rales and dullness to percussion in the lower lung fields bilaterally. Sensory and motor examination was grossly intact.
Laboratory data revealed white blood count 13,900/mcL, hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelets 370,000/mcL, sodium 131 mmol/L potassium 5.8 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L, carbon dioxide 17 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 155 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 8.9 mg/dL. Arterial blood gases showed a pH of 7.39, pCO2 32.2 mmHg, bicarbonate 19.1 mmol/L, and pO2 74.5 mmHg on 3 L nasal cannula. Chest X-ray showed diffuse bilateral reticulonodular opacities (Figure 1). He was found to be HIV positive with CD4 count of <5 cells/cc and viral load of 1,180,000 copies. Bronchoalveolar lavage was preformed; Grocott's methenamine silver stain of the washings demonstrated Pneumocystis jiroveci (Figure 2). He received antibiotics and steroids with gradual improvement.
On hospital day 14, he became confused and acutely developed nystagmus with both a horizontal and prominent vertical component. He was also found to have ataxia with finger to nose testing and difficulty sitting up without support. Considering his immunosuppressed state, infectious and neoplastic etiologies were the primary diagnostic considerations. Lumbar puncture revealed clear CSF, normal opening pressure, and normal cell counts. Polymerase chain reactions for Epstein-Barr virus, Herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, and John Cunningham (JC) virus were negative. Nontreponemal serological screening for syphilis (VDRL), toxoplasmosis antibody, and Cryptococcus antigen titers were negative. CT of the head did not show any intracranial mass, hemorrhage, or other acute findings. MRI of the brain revealed a slight increase in T2 signal within the medial aspect of thalamus bilaterally (Figure 3). After excluding infection and neoplasm, the clinical diagnosis of Wernicke's encephalopathy was made. Intravenous thiamine was administered resulting in resolution of symptoms, which confirmed the diagnosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old male presenting with progressive dyspnea and productive cough for 4 months, accompanied by anorexia and a 50-pound weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed progressive shortness of breath and productive cough over four months, with profound anorexia and a 50-pound weight loss over five months. Two months prior, he ceased cigarette smoking due to worsening respiratory distress. On presentation, he was in respiratory failure. While hospitalized and improving on antimicrobial therapy, he acutely developed horizontal and vertical nystagmus, appendicular ataxia, and truncal instability on hospital day 14.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical or surgical history; no prior hospitalizations; prior military service in Hawaii with heterosexual commercial sex worker exposure; former tobacco smoker (quit 2 months prior); rare alcohol use; denied illicit substance use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for productive cough, progressive dyspnea, anorexia, 50-lb weight loss, acute nystagmus, and gait imbalance; negative for fever, night sweats, or hemoptysis initially. Home medications: none. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vitals: Temperature: 99.9 °F, blood pressure: 128/83 mmHg, pulse: 134 beats/min, respiratory rate: 22 breaths/min, SpO2: 92% on room air. General: moderate respiratory distress, awake and cooperative. HEENT: oral thrush under tongue and on palate; pupils equal and reactive; no icterus. Neck: no lymphadenopathy. Lungs: diminished breath sounds bilaterally with crackles/rales and dullness to percussion at lung bases. Day 14 neurologic exam: confused, bilateral horizontal and prominent vertical nystagmus, dysmetria on bilateral finger-to-nose testing, truncal ataxia with inability to sit unsupported.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: WBC 13,900/mcL, hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelets 370,000/mcL. Serum chemistry: sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L, BUN 155 mg/dL, serum creatinine 8.9 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas (3 L nasal cannula): pH 7.39, pCO2 32.2 mmHg, HCO3- 19.1 mmol/L, pO2 74.5 mmHg. Chest X-ray: diffuse bilateral reticulonodular opacities. Non-treponemal syphilis test (VDRL): negative; toxoplasmosis serology: negative; serum Cryptococcus antigen: negative. Lumbar puncture: clear CSF, normal opening pressure, normal cell count; CSF PCR for EBV, HSV, CMV, and JC virus: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) stain demonstrated Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts and trophozoites. Non-contrast head CT: normal, no intracranial mass or hemorrhage. Brain MRI: increased T2/FLAIR hyperintensity within the medial aspect of the bilateral thalami.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) and acute severe renal failure in newly diagnosed advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) / AIDS (CD4 count < 5 cells/mcL, viral load 1,180,000 copies/mL), complicated on day 14 by Wernicke encephalopathy triggered by malnutrition and refeeding. CNS infections (PML, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, CMV, HSV, EBV, neurosyphilis) and CNS lymphoma ruled out by normal CSF, negative PCRs, and characteristic bilateral medial thalamic T2 hyperintensities on MRI. Management & Outcome: Treated with high-dose intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and adjunctive systemic corticosteroids with gradual pulmonary improvement. At onset of neurological signs on day 14, prompt administration of high-dose intravenous thiamine resulted in complete resolution of encephalopathy, nystagmus, and ataxia, confirming Wernicke encephalopathy.
